title: Python is missing on this PC
story: A session found no usable python on this PC and wrote the fix down. Ten minutes after a compaction dropped the 'no Python' line, a top model typed a python heredoc again.
entry: Python or python3 exits 49 (Microsoft Store stub). A real Python 3.12.14 sits in the Codex app folder. Call that full path, or use node or PowerShell for small JSON work. Check: the path with --version prints 3.12.14.
steps: The window points toward Python, because CLAUDE.md names Python 3.12. A summary that said 'no Python' was replaced by one without it.
The design names no trigger. A shell tool error is not one of the listed triggers. Only the exit-49 result could start a lookup, and that comes after the call.
The error text is word for word and easy to recognise.
This is the main session. The entry is held until the next compaction, and this session already lost the fact once at a compaction.
Swap python for the full path. A plain JSON script runs on 3.12.
The rerun's exit code decides, at no cost.
The failing model is already the top rung. A stronger model would make the same call.

The first solver was building a link graph. Python was a side stumble, not the problem solved. The design needs a fix commit and a control pair, and a PC fact has neither. The fact reached memory 29 days later.
The interpreter belongs to another app, which rewrote its folder on 2026-10-21. Newer Pythons arrived later. No repository event marks any of this.

title: Python error, but this project uses uv
story: A subagent typed bare python while its window held the project's 'uv run --locked python' route. It failed, then recovered with diff and grep on the next call.
entry: Same as the python entry, or the memory line: python is not on PATH in Git Bash (Windows Store alias); use node for JSON.
steps: The project's right route, uv run, was already in the window. The agent typed bare python anyway.
Same as before. No trigger fires before the call.
The error text is the same word for word.
Same error, different right answer. The entry says node or Codex 3.12. This project uses uv with locked 3.13 packages.
The subagent window holds it for its short life.
Fine for a JSON compare. For anything that imports project code it points to the wrong interpreter and away from uv run.
No rule says whether the clinic variant is stored as a sibling, a revision, or not at all.
Two project memories now disagree about one PC. EMS says use node for JSON. The clinic says uv run python. The design has no project field.

title: A stored 'no' about tools that exist
story: A design note said no Python and no gh on this PC. Six minutes later gh was installed. Python had been in use since 10-06. Clinic memory later stored 'no uv' and uv was then installed.
entry: No Python and no gh on this PC. Design around them. Run backend gates only in Docker.
steps: A session planning work here would look up which tools exist.
No error occurs when an agent avoids a tool it wrongly believes is missing.
'Is there Python?' is a plain-language question. Only plain-language handles could match it.
The entry is returned. That is the problem.
The cheap model designs around tools that exist, such as Docker-only gates. Nothing it does fails.
A stored 'no' never fails loudly. The agent just does not try. Only a separate review caught it on 11-01.
There is no failure to hand up.
The writer checked PATH only. It wrote 'no gh' six minutes before installing gh, and 'no Python' while Python had been in use since 10-06.
Agents change the PC. gh arrived 10-31, uv on 11-02. Corrections landed separately in a doc, a memory note and the design. The clinic copy is still stale.

title: Bash cuts long heredoc commands
story: Bash commands over about 8 KB fail with an unexpected-EOF error and write nothing. Four later moments repeated it, once by the note's own writer a day after writing it.
entry: Bash cat heredoc fails 'unexpected EOF while looking for matching quote' at about 9,800 characters, and the file is not written. The tool cuts long commands. Write the file with the Write tool. Dead end: re-sending the heredoc.
steps: The entry is in the window, pushed at start. So is the Bash tool's own advice to use a heredoc for multi-line text. They pull opposite ways.
The cost is the failed call itself, 8.6k to 18.6k characters sent twice. A lookup can only follow the error. Nothing fires before the call.
'unexpected EOF while looking for matching' is word for word.
It was delivered by push into main and subagent windows. The pull-only route in the other design would deliver less.
The note was present and not applied in four moments, once by its own writer. The condition is the length of the agent's own next output, which it does not measure.
Sonnet, Opus and Fable all fail the same way.
First failure was 10-31. The note came on 11-11 after the 40-error peak day, in a batch memory edit, not at a solve.
The limit belongs to the tool version, not a repository. No footprint item sees a tool upgrade.

title: Four agents, same long command, same day
story: Four Opus agents each wrote four slide files in one cat command of 10 to 11k characters and all failed within six seconds. One recovered with four Reads and four Writes.
entry: The Bash heredoc entry from the previous case. That project's memory has no Bash note.
steps: This is a different project's memory. It has nothing about Bash limits.
As before, the cost comes before any trigger.
The error text is word for word.
It hits only if the library is shared across projects. The owner says it is. The other design is silent.
Four windows opened six seconds apart. No sibling could finish, record and serve another in time.
Four equal solvers of one stumble. The design does not say who writes, or how four near-duplicates merge.

title: Read cannot open PDF pages here
source: Session e56a900a, parent and wave-2 agents
story: Read on a PDF failed because pdftoppm is missing. The parent found a PowerShell route. Five hours later four new Opus agents hit the same error, because the briefs never mentioned PDFs.
entry: Read with pages on a PDF fails: pdftoppm is not installed. Python is the Store stub. Route: PowerShell reads the bytes, inflates FlateDecode streams and pulls the text. Works for the 41-page Google Docs PDF. Avoid the reserved variable $PID.
steps: The brief, written by a parent that knew, has no word 'pdf'. Wave 1 hit the error four seconds before the parent did.
A Read tool error is not on the list of triggers.
The error text is word for word.
This works if the parent's route was stored by 14:16Z.
The stored route took the parent three tries and 113.6 KB of output. Some agents found cheaper pre-extracted text. The entry may pull toward the costlier route.
Text appears or it does not.
Parent and children were all Opus and all failed alike.
It was solved as an aside. There is no mid-session capture point. Wave 2 started 5.5 hours later with nothing written. No note ever recorded pdftoppm.
The route depends on how the PDF was made. Pre-extracted text exists for some files in one project only.

title: PDF route, in another project, a month on
story: Research subagents read saved PDFs. The brief named the Codex Python. A Sonnet agent extracted the text in two calls using pypdf. An Opus agent gave up on the PDF.
entry: The PDF entry from the previous case: PowerShell inflate, or the clinic's pre-extracted text folder.
steps: The brief carried a PC fact that was half of the answer.
The error text is word for word.
It returns the clinic route. Its text folder does not exist in this repository, and inflate fits some PDFs only.
The best route needs the PDF entry joined with the Python fact. Sonnet made the join unaided. Opus gave up on the source.
Pages of text appear or they do not.
Sonnet solved it. Opus did not.
Who records the pypdf route, as a sibling or a revision, is not said.
pypdf lives in another app's private runtime, which that app rewrote on 10-21. A stored path to it can change with no event here.

title: Git 'Filename too long' in the scratchpad
story: Refuters cloning repos in the scratchpad hit Windows' 260-character path limit. Six refused alone on 11-03. Next day 15 of 15 clones failed. The tool then shortened the path.
entry: git add, clone or cherry-pick in the scratchpad fails 'Filename too long'. The scratchpad path is about 170 characters. In the throwaway repo run git config core.longpaths true. Check: git add -A succeeds.
steps: Refuters were building throwaway repos in the scratchpad. Nothing in their window mentioned it.
A git error in a scratch repo is not a listed trigger.
'Filename too long' is word for word.
Siblings run in parallel. A mid-workflow entry reaches only agents started after it, and only by pull.
git add succeeds or it does not.
None of the six had capture duty. Each got out alone. The note came next day from another session after 15 more failures.
A tool update removed the cause about three hours after the note. The note still says the path is about 170 characters. No repository event marks a tool change.

title: 'Name too long' with a different cause
source: Clinic Opus 11-01; two Sonnet agents 11-04; Codex Sonnet 11-10
story: 'ENAMETOOLONG' came from commands over Windows' 32,767-character line limit, not from paths. Two of these contain no git at all.
entry: The git longpaths entry and the Bash heredoc entry.
steps: Agents pasted very large scripts into one Bash call.
The error words name a path. The cause is command length. The query carries the wrong cause.
'name too long' is a piece of 'Filename too long'. The design matches template fragments, so the git entry is the hit. The right family shares no word.
The git flag cannot shorten a 40k command. A shorter scratchpad path does not either.
The rerun fails again, one wasted call before real diagnosis.
The agents' own fix, shorter commands and then Write, was never recorded.
After the path change the git entry is stale for its own symptom, yet still matches this one.

title: A constant-time compare copied to a webhook
story: The ops token gate used hmac.compare_digest on text. Seven days later the same pattern guarded the WhatsApp webhook. A non-ASCII byte turns it into a server error. Review found it 20 days on.
entry: Ops proxy-token gate. A FastAPI dependency reads X-Ops-Proxy-Token. 401 if unset. Constant-time compare with hmac.compare_digest(x or '', expected). 401 on mismatch. Router tests for right, wrong and missing token pass.
steps: The later author had the ops gate file in the repository either way.
Nothing failed. Writing new code is not a trigger. The diff warning fires only on stored hazards, and none existed before 07-28.
If asked, 'constant-time compare of a webhook token' is a plain-language query.
It returns the ops gate solution, which contains the defect, stored as solved by a top model.
Copying the stored pattern spreads the defect to a public webhook. That is what happened without a library.
Tests passed. Output equal to the strong model's was the defect.
Both writers were the top rung of their day. The bug surfaced only through a later review.
The 07-28 fix is a clean capture: a safe helper, seven helper tests, per-site tests and a CLAUDE.md rule. It can be stored as a do-not-apply entry.
The handle hmac.compare_digest also fires on the safe PIN check. Stored tests cover the three fixed sites, not a new site. The JavaScript variant shares no identifier.

title: Subagents refused report files
story: A clinic note said subagents cannot write report files. Eleven days later in EMS, eight subagents were refused for report.md, while 22 other .md files and 156 .js files were written fine.
entry: Subagents cannot write report files; the harness refuses. Ask them to return the full result in their reply. Earlier Sonnet extractors did write files, so the refusal may depend on agent type or output size.
steps: The brief, written by the main session, asks for report.md.
The error fires in the subagent. Its cause is the brief in the main session, which sees no error and has no trigger.
The error text is word for word.
The entry's condition, agent type or output size, is wrong. The record points to the file name.
It is delivered to the one window that cannot change the brief.
Return text. The error message already says so, so the library adds nothing.
It was captured the same day but too broadly. The writer had two refusals and one counter-example and could not tell which detail mattered.
It was stored in clinic memory only, and EMS repeated it eleven days later. Read as 'subagents cannot write files', it would push other file writes into replies too.
